source.title: Q-realign: Piggybacking Realignment on Quantization for Safe and Efficient LLM Deployment
source.authors: Qi-Tao Tan; Xiao-Ying Song; Ning-Xi Cheng; Ninghao Liu; Xiao-Ming Zhai; Ling-Zi Hong; Yan-Zhi Wang; Zhen Xiang; Geng Yuan

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes aligned chat models using benign and varying-ratio harmful data, then measures harmful outputs and refusal behavior, directly testing safety degradation after fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports Q-realign and baseline defense results, but those results concern post-fine-tuning defenses and do not test the claim about first-token concentration, bypassing an opening, localized safety parameters, or training that deepens safety by response position. The layer-wise refusal measurements are included because they directly measure refusal on malicious inputs before and after fine-tuning.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but its vanilla SFT baselines report harmful scores on AdvBench for aligned chat models after LoRA fine-tuning. These cover clean Alpaca and Alpaca mixed with 5–20% harmful samples, plus SST-2 and GSM8K. The method differs from the originals: LoRA, harmful-ratio mixtures, a trained harmfulness classifier, and a Lisa/Panacea-style protocol. Those baseline numbers bear directly on V1 and V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that fine-tuning, even benign, raises unsafe behaviour. They conjecture this stems from lost separability of benign and malicious intermediate activations. They present Q-realign, a post-training-quantization defense that restores separability and cuts harmful scores (e.g., 40.38 to 7.88) while preserving task accuracy and costing far less compute than baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tests aligned-model fine-tuning with varying harmful ratios and harmful-output evaluation, including clean fine-tuning. It uses LoRA and reports harmful scores; the number of training examples is not stated. Q-realign itself is a post-training quantization defense, not part of the fine-tuning intervention tested here.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported harmful score changes with the fine-tuning harmful ratio and dataset; the paper reports different scores for Alpaca, SST-2, and GSM8K settings.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning, the Fisher separability of benign versus malicious intermediate activations drops across most layers, more so with a higher harmful ratio. Refusal when decoding from intermediate layers also falls, below 20% at layer 30 for hr=0.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning degrades the representational separation of harmful and benign inputs across layers, alongside increased harmful compliance.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Harmful scores are evaluated with a trained classifier; refusal detection for layer-wise decoding uses keywords. The paper says results are averages of three runs but reports no error bars or other uncertainty estimates. It does not state harmful-example counts, and some cross-model and dataset results lack aligned-model comparison scores.
record.rows_left_out: Defense-method results in Tables 1–5, including Q-realign, are omitted because they measure post-fine-tuning defense outcomes rather than the claim versions about fine-tuning-induced degradation mechanisms, first-token concentration, bypasses, or safety depth.

untested.parts: The absolute number of harmful examples (only ratios are given; dataset size is unstated); full-parameter fine-tuning; closed models.
Selected or adversarially chosen benign data; benign data other than Alpaca (the SST-2 and GSM8K runs appear to include harmful samples).
Not tested; no per-token KL analysis.
Not tested; no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested. The authors conjecture a loss of activation separability, but this concerns fine-tuning degradation, not token-depth shallowness.
Not tested. Q-realign is a quantization-based recovery and is not evaluated by response position.

missing.what: Layer-wise Fisher separability ratio before and after fine-tuning (clean and hr=0.05)
Harmful ratio used for the SST-2, GSM8K and cross-model fine-tuning runs, and pre-fine-tuning harmful scores for Gemma2-9B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-it
missing.locator: Tables 2–3; Section 4.2 (not reported by the paper)

record.verdict_notes: Treat the V1/V2 evidence as baseline numbers inside a defense paper. Harmfulness is judged by the Huang et al. (2023) classifier on an AdvBench subset, with no error bars. The reader's V2 supports and limits_scope labels for the same condition are merged into one limits_scope label. The r6 and r7 links are moved to V1 because the paper frames all dataset runs as fine-tuning attacks with malicious portions. The SFT baseline is described ambiguously: Appendix B.2 says quantization is applied, but Section 4.1 and the FP16 row of the bit-width table indicate floating point.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state the number of harmful training examples, so it does not establish the claimed range of a few to a few hundred examples.

The paper tests clean Alpaca fine-tuning and reports outcomes for SST-2 and GSM8K fine-tunes, but does not provide aligned-model comparison scores for SST-2 or GSM8K or test specially selected benign examples.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models is reported.
No compliant prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test is reported.
The study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study proposes representational separability as a mechanism for fine-tuning-related safety degradation, but does not test why safety would be shallow across response tokens.
Q-realign restores safety-related behavior using quantization, but the study does not train or test safety distributed beyond the first response tokens or its robustness at response positions.

rows.note: The text identifies this as benign fine-tuning and reports the aligned pre-trained score as 0.0. The increase is much smaller than the harmful-data fine-tuning results.

rows.subject: LLaMA2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Layer-wise decoding of intermediate activations on malicious inputs

conditions.value: middle and upper layers, e.g. layer 20+

rows.value: Nearly all malicious inputs are refused
rows.note: This is the aligned reference condition for the paper's comparison with fine-tuned models.
rows.check: This measures keyword refusal when decoding directly from intermediate-layer activations, not the model's actual output behaviour. It is a related representational construct, not harmful compliance.

rows.subject: LLaMA2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning with harmful data, followed by layer-wise decoding of intermediate activations
rows.baseline: Aligned pre-trained model refuses nearly all inputs in middle and upper layers, e.g. layer 20+
rows.note: The text says the fine-tuned model fails to reliably refuse malicious inputs even at a later layer.
rows.check: Same as r10: intermediate-layer decoding refusal (<20% at layer 30, hr=0.05) is not the model's output compliance. The actual output effect is already captured by r2.
